title: Josaphat (12 November)
hookLine: a Ukrainian Greek Catholic archbishop killed in the struggles over unity

lines: A PRAYER ON THE LAST NIGHT.
THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
cards: On the night before he dies, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays out loud for his friends, then for people who will believe later, people he'll never meet in the flesh.

He asks one thing for all of them: "That they all may be one." Christians have carried that line a long time, and they haven't always kept it. Sometimes the arguments over what unity means have been fierce.
Today's saint lived inside one of those arguments, and it cost him his life: a monk from the lands of Ukraine and Belarus who became an archbishop.

teach.b: Josaphat grew up in the Eastern Christian world: icons, the Byzantine liturgy sung in Church Slavonic, married parish priests, long fasts.

teach.h: UNION WITH ROME, AND A SPLIT.
teach.b: In his time some bishops of that church entered into union with the bishop of Rome. They kept their own liturgy, their own customs, their own way of praying, and they accepted the pope's authority.
Others refused, and stayed with the Orthodox Church. Families, towns and parishes were split. Josaphat became a monk, then archbishop of Polotsk, on the side of the union.
He preached, he cared for the poor, and he worked hard to bring people into the union he believed in. Here's the honest part.
The struggle was bitter, and historians record harsh pressure and anger on more than one side. Josaphat was killed by a crowd in a town of his diocese, by people opposed to the union.
The Catholic Church honors him as a martyr.

Orthodox Christians remember those same years with their own wounds, and the two churches still tell that history differently. That's why his feast can be a hard one, and why today's practice isn't about winning.
Today Catholic and Orthodox Christians meet, talk and sometimes pray together.
The Eastern Catholic churches, like the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church that especially honors Josaphat, hold two things together: an Eastern way of worship and communion with Rome.
His life asks what unity costs, and who pays it.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Josaphat on 12 November; Ukrainian Greek Catholics and other Eastern Catholics honor him with particular devotion, and Catholics often pray for Christian unity on his feast.

o: an Orthodox patriarch who refused union with Rome

games.q: you're a Christian in Josaphat's lands, and your town is split over union with Rome. a neighbor on the other side is in need. what do you do?
o: ignore them until they change sides.
games.why: there's no single answer in the record for neighbors; the record shows how bitter the split became, and both churches still carry it.

practice: Bring to mind Christians who are not like each other: a Catholic parish, an Orthodox church with its icons, a Protestant congregation down the road.
Pick the one you know least, name one thing its people love, a hymn, a fast, a saint, and let it stand on its own, with no comparison.
If you pray, pray the line from John's Gospel, that they all may be one; if not, simply wish that community well.

wordCard.voice: Josaphat. An Eastern Catholic monk and archbishop of Polotsk, killed in the struggle over union with Rome, and honored by the Catholic Church as a martyr.

orig.note: Ukrainian: Josaphat, his name in religious life, after a king of Judah.
